questions.q: A researcher places a red dot on the nose of a 14-month-old infant and places the infant in front of a mirror. The infant reaches out to touch the dot on the mirror reflection. What does this behaviour indicate about the infant's self-awareness?
questions.a: The infant lacks self-awareness; touching the reflection indicates the infant perceives the mirror image as another child, not as themselves. Self-awareness is demonstrated only when the infant touches their own nose. A wrong answer (e.g., "the infant is self-aware because they noticed the dot") reveals confusion between visual attention and self-recognition, missing the critical distinction between "that is me" vs "that is another baby."

questions.q: Four-year-old Arjun describes himself: "I have a red cycle. I can run fast. I am never scared. I am a good boy." Identify which THREE of the five early childhood self-description characteristics (from NCERT) are illustrated in Arjun's statements.
questions.a: Arjun shows: (1) Physical/material descriptions ("red cycle"), (2) Active descriptions ("run fast"), (3) Absolute/non-comparative terms ("fast" not "faster than"), (4) Overestimation ("never scared"), and (5) Inability to hold contradictory traits ("good boy" only). Any three correctly identified with mapping to statements is correct. A wrong answer listing "social comparison" or "psychological traits" reveals the misconception that early childhood self-understanding resembles middle childhood.

questions.q: Nine-year-old Priya says: "I am good at making friends. I am in the school choir. I can finish homework faster than my brother. I want to be a doctor but I am not smart enough yet." Map each statement to the correct middle childhood characteristic: (a) internal psychological traits, (b) social identity/group membership, (c) social comparison, (d) real vs ideal self distinction.
questions.a: Mapping: "good at making friends" → (a) internal psychological traits; "school choir" → (b) social identity; "faster than my brother" → (c) social comparison; "want to be a doctor but not smart enough" → (d) real vs ideal self. A wrong answer confusing (a) and (b) (e.g., calling choir an internal trait) reveals failure to distinguish personal attributes from group-based definitions.

questions.q: Compare the self-descriptions of a 3-year-old ("I have a big truck") and a 10-year-old ("I am generous but sometimes selfish"). Analyze how the shift from concrete/absolute to abstract/contradictory descriptions reflects cognitive development, referencing the role of perspective-taking ability.
questions.a: The 3-year-old uses concrete, observable possessions in absolute terms (characteristic of preoperational thought). The 10-year-old uses abstract psychological traits ("generous") and acknowledges contradictions ("sometimes selfish"), reflecting concrete operational thought enabling perspective-taking and realistic self-evaluation. A wrong answer attributing the change solely to "vocabulary growth" misses the cognitive structural shift (decentration, reversibility) that permits multi-dimensional self-views.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: "The mirror test at 18 months proves the infant has a fully formed self-concept." Use the distinction between self-awareness (implicit) and self-concept (explicit, verbalizable) to justify your position.
questions.a: The claim is false. Mirror test shows implicit self-awareness (bodily self, agency) — a pre-verbal, non-conceptual sense of "me as object." Self-concept requires explicit, verbalizable self-descriptions ("I am...") which emerge only with language in early childhood. A wrong answer agreeing with the claim conflates the *onset* of self-awareness with the *construction* of self-concept, ignoring the developmental gap between 18 months and 3+ years.

questions.q: Design a 3-item interview protocol to distinguish whether a 5-year-old and an 8-year-old are operating at early childhood vs middle childhood level of self-understanding. Each item must target a different NCERT characteristic.
questions.a: Sample protocol: (1) "Tell me about yourself" → code for physical/material (early) vs psychological/internal (middle). (2) "Are you good at drawing?" → follow with "Better than your friend?" → absolute (early) vs comparative (middle). (3) "Can you be naughty and nice?" → "No, I'm always good" (early) vs "Yes, sometimes" (middle). A poor protocol uses only one question or targets non-distinguishing features (e.g., "What's your name?").
